objectives: Distinguish El Niño + La Niña + neutral states.
Connect ENSO to global climate variability.

slides.title: ENSO: the master mode of interannual climate variability
slides.body:
**El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)**: coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific, with global teleconnections. The dominant mode of natural climate variability on years-to-decade timescales.

Two phases + a neutral:
• **Neutral**: normal trade winds push warm surface water westward across Pacific; cold water upwells off Peru/Ecuador; Walker circulation: rising air over western Pacific (Indonesia), descending over eastern Pacific.
• **El Niño**: trade winds weaken / reverse; warm pool shifts eastward; upwelling off South America declines; surface T anomalies in eastern Pacific +1 to +3 °C. Walker circulation weakens or reverses.
• **La Niña**: trades intensify; warm pool retreats westward; upwelling stronger; eastern Pacific surface T anomalies -1 to -2 °C.

Oscillation period: 2-7 years irregularly. Phase transitions take ~months. ENSO state monitored via:
- **Niño-3.4 index**: SST anomaly 5°N-5°S, 120-170°W. Used by NOAA + WMO.
- **Southern Oscillation Index (SOI)**: pressure difference Tahiti minus Darwin.
- Other indices: Niño-1+2, Niño-3, Niño-4, Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI).

**Major historical events**:
- 1982-83 El Niño: strongest then-recorded.
- 1997-98 El Niño: very strong, global impacts.
- 2009-10 El Niño Modoki: central-Pacific variant.
- 2015-16 El Niño: strong + record global temperatures.
- 2023-24 El Niño: strong; coincided with record global heat.

ENSO drives ~15-50% of global interannual temperature variability + larger fractions of regional precipitation.

slides.title: Bjerknes feedback + dynamic coupling
slides.body:
**Bjerknes (1969) feedback** explains why ENSO oscillates rather than dampens:

*Initial perturbation*: weakening of trade winds (random / triggered).

*Step 1*: weak winds → less westward push of surface water → warm pool extends eastward → SST rises in eastern Pacific.

*Step 2*: warm SST anomaly in east → atmospheric convection shifts east → low surface pressure in east, high in west.

*Step 3*: pressure gradient further weakens trade winds in east.

*Step 4*: feedback loop: weak winds → warm SST → weak winds → ... → El Niño develops.

This is a **positive (amplifying) feedback**, but it terminates because:
• Thermocline shoaling in west builds up potential energy.
• Equatorial Kelvin waves carry cold thermocline anomaly eastward.
• Reflected Rossby waves help cool the eastern Pacific.
• La Niña conditions can develop after the El Niño phase, completing oscillation.

Mechanistically detailed by the **'delayed oscillator'** theory + the **'recharge oscillator'** + extensions. ENSO is now intensively studied as a coupled phenomenon — atmospheric circulation + ocean thermocline + heat-budget perspectives all required.

**ENSO is NOT periodic** — it's a stochastic oscillation with characteristic timescales 2-7 yr. Each event has unique structure + duration. This complicates prediction; forecast skill ~6-12 months ahead with ENSO models (CFSv2, ECMWF SEAS, etc.).

slides.title: Global teleconnections + climate impact
slides.body:
ENSO has remote effects via atmospheric Rossby-wave propagation + altered Hadley + Walker circulations:

• **United States**: El Niño → wetter winters in southern tier (CA, AZ, FL); drier in PNW. La Niña → drier in southern US + wet in PNW. Drives flood + drought + agricultural impacts.
• **South America**: El Niño → severe drought in NE Brazil + Amazon; wet + floods in Peru + Ecuador. Reversed in La Niña.
• **Indonesia + Australia**: El Niño → drought (Indonesia, eastern Australia); fires. La Niña → wet + floods (2010-11 Queensland, 2022 Pakistan + Australia).
• **East Africa**: El Niño → wet (Kenya, Somalia, Tanzania); La Niña → drought (Horn of Africa).
• **Indian monsoon**: El Niño → drier monsoon (years of weak monsoon coincide with El Niño).
• **Atlantic hurricanes**: El Niño → fewer hurricanes (vertical shear suppresses). La Niña → more hurricanes (favorable shear).
• **Global mean T**: El Niño year → average ~0.1-0.2 °C warmer than neutral. 2016, 2023, 2024 (super-El-Niño years) were record-hot globally.

**Economic impacts**:
- 1997-98 El Niño: ~$40B economic damages globally.
- 2015-16: similar magnitude.
- Agricultural + fisheries impacts: Peruvian anchovy fishery (collapsed during El Niños); global crop yields (US, Australia, India).
- Insurance, energy demand (heating/cooling), tourism all affected.

**Climate-change interaction**: how does anthropogenic warming affect ENSO? CMIP6 models split between:
- More frequent / intense El Niños (more variable Pacific).
- Less frequent but more extreme.
- Little change.
Observations: super-El-Niños (1982-83, 1997-98, 2015-16, 2023-24) may be more frequent recently — possibly an emerging climate change signal. Still active research.

**Prediction + forecasting**:
- IRI / NOAA Climate Prediction Center provide official ENSO forecasts.
- ENSO + monthly-to-seasonal forecasts inform: water management, agriculture, public health (mosquito-borne disease anticipation), disaster preparedness.
- ML-based ENSO forecasts (Ham+ 2019, transformer-based) achieving 18+ month lead time.

question.question: Walk through the 2015-16 El Niño event
question.goal: Trace the development + global impacts of the 2015-16 El Niño event (one of the strongest on record).

steps.prompt: Early 2015: precursor signals. What did the equatorial Pacific look like?
steps.reveal: Early 2015 (Jan-Mar): Westerly Wind Bursts (WWBs) east of the dateline triggered downwelling Kelvin waves propagating eastward. Thermocline deepened in central Pacific; warm SST anomalies began forming.

steps.prompt: By mid-2015: how did Niño-3.4 evolve?
steps.reveal: Niño-3.4 SST anomaly grew from +0.5 °C (Jan) to +2.0 °C (Jul), continuing through summer/fall. WMO officially declared El Niño in spring 2015.

Peak Niño-3.4: +2.9 °C in November 2015 — one of the three strongest events recorded (1982-83 and 1997-98 also reached ~+2.7 to +2.9 °C). Anomalously warm pool extended ~150° longitude. Global mean SST set records.

acceptedAnswers: Indonesia drought, US wetter, Pakistan flooding, Caribbean hurricanes

steps.reveal:
Among impacts:
- **Indonesia**: severe drought + peatland + forest fires (~$16B economic damage; massive haze across SE Asia).
- **California**: above-average winter rain (some drought relief).
- **Ethiopia + Horn of Africa**: severe drought (~10 million food-insecure).
- **Peru + Ecuador**: heavy rains + flooding.
- **Caribbean + Atlantic**: fewer hurricanes than usual (high shear).
- **Pacific cyclones**: 2 of the strongest cyclones recorded (Patricia in E. Pacific, Winston in S. Pacific) during this period.
- **Global mean T**: 2015 + 2016 set successive global-temperature records; +0.15-0.2 °C boost from ENSO over base trend.

Economic damages from 2015-16 ENSO: ~$30-50B globally; ~60 million people food-insecure due to drought/flood impacts.

steps.prompt: Post-peak: La Niña developed in 2016. Why?
hints: Stored heat anomaly drained; cold anomaly returned.
steps.reveal: After peak, thermocline shoaling in central + eastern Pacific (cold anomaly rising); equatorial Rossby waves carry cooling westward; reflection as Kelvin waves brings cold anomaly back east. By mid-2016, weak La Niña conditions developed (Niño-3.4 ~-0.5 to -1 °C). This 2-year cycle (2015 El Niño → 2016 La Niña) is typical ENSO pattern — though not periodic.

question.question: Classify each regional impact as occurring during an El Niño or La Niña event (or both/neither).

items.label: Heavy rains + floods in coastal Peru
Wet winters in Pacific Northwest US
Drought in Horn of Africa (E. Africa)

question.explanation:
ENSO teleconnection patterns are well-established by physical mechanism + observation:
• El Niño: Walker circulation weakens → western Pacific drier (Indonesia drought, Australian fires), eastern Pacific wetter (Peru floods). Hadley cell shifts → US sub-tropical jet strengthens → wetter southern US. Vertical shear weakens Atlantic hurricanes. Indian monsoon weakens. East Africa wetter.
• La Niña: opposite — Indonesia + Australia wet; Pacific NW wet; southern US drier; Atlantic hurricanes more active; East Africa (Horn) drier.

These patterns are statistical — not every El Niño produces every impact, but the probability-shifts inform climate-services forecasting. Modern climate-prediction centers issue regional outlooks at 1-6 month lead times based on ENSO state + other modes (NAO, IOD, AMO).

question.question: Why is ENSO prediction reliable at 6-12 months lead time but unreliable beyond 18 months?
options: ENSO has an 'inherent predictability' set by the thermocline-Kelvin-wave timescale (~6-12 months) + the ocean-atmosphere coupling. Beyond that, small-scale weather noise + the 'spring predictability barrier' (transitions occur in northern-spring, when ENSO state is ambiguous + sensitive to perturbations) limit deterministic forecasts. Recent ML methods (transformer-based, deep ensembles) push to ~18-22 months by extracting weak signals; further requires fundamentally new approaches.
question.explanation:
**ENSO predictability mechanism**:

1. **Subsurface memory**: warm/cold water anomalies in the thermocline propagate as Kelvin + Rossby waves. Persist + slowly translate over months → forecastable.

2. **Atmospheric coupling**: Walker circulation + trade-wind anomalies maintain ENSO state through Bjerknes feedback. Couples ocean + atmosphere on intra-seasonal timescales.

3. **Spring predictability barrier**: equatorial Pacific T anomalies transition in northern spring (Apr-Jun) when monsoonal + global circulation patterns are weak. Initial-condition errors amplify across this window. Forecasts initialized in Jan-Feb (pre-barrier) have lower skill at 6-month lead than those initialized in Jun-Jul (post-barrier).

4. **Stochastic forcing**: Westerly Wind Bursts (WWBs), Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), volcanic eruptions perturb ENSO. These have limited predictability themselves.

5. **Model limitations**: coupled GCMs (NCEP CFSv2, ECMWF SEAS, NMME ensemble) have biases — too-strong amplitude, wrong west-east SST gradient, weak/strong asymmetry between El Niño + La Niña. Continuously updated.

**Forecast skill (verified)**:
- 1-3 months: high skill (Niño-3.4 R > 0.8 between forecast + observation).
- 6-9 months: moderate skill (R ~ 0.6-0.7); reliable for risk assessment.
- 12-18 months: low-moderate skill; useful for risk planning but not deterministic.
- > 18 months: research frontier; some studies claim skill via ML/transformer approaches but contested.

**Ham+ 2019** (Nature): deep-learning approach using SST + heat content fields reached 1.5-year-ahead forecasts at skill levels exceeding traditional models. Subsequent transformer-based methods extending this. Whether genuinely new mechanism or improved extraction of existing signals — debated.

**Operational ENSO products**:
- NOAA Climate Prediction Center: monthly ENSO discussion (since 1990s); diagnostic + outlook.
- IRI (International Research Institute): ENSO + Quick Look prediction plumes; multi-model ensemble.
- WMO: regional climate outlook forums every 3-6 months.

**Practical use**: 6-12 month lead ENSO information used for: water-resource planning, crop-insurance pricing, disaster preparedness (flood/drought), public health (mosquito-borne disease forecasts), energy markets, fishery management.

Forecasts have substantial economic value even at imperfect skill; ENSO is one of the most-policy-relevant climate signals.

slides.workedSolution: ENSO has inherent predictability from thermocline memory (Kelvin + Rossby waves; ~6-12 month timescales) + ocean-atmosphere coupling (Bjerknes). Spring predictability barrier (Apr-Jun) limits forecasts initialized before; post-barrier forecasts more skillful. Model limitations + stochastic forcing (WWBs, MJO) cap useful skill at ~18 months for current methods. ML approaches (Ham+ 2019) push to 18+ months. ENSO forecasts used for water, crop, disaster, public health, energy applications worldwide.

question.question: If a strong El Niño boosts global temperature by ~0.15 °C above neutral, and underlying anthropogenic warming is ~0.02 °C/yr, what year-on-year temperature jump might 2024 (super-El-Niño) show over 2023 (also El-Niño)?
question.hint: If both ENSO-influenced, mostly underlying trend dominates. ~0.02-0.05 °C typical.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how ENSO acts as both a 'natural variability mode' + a 'climate-change-sensitive process'.
question.rubric: Mentions: ENSO is natural variability — coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in tropical Pacific; existed pre-industrially (paleoclimate records show ENSO present at least back to last glacial period). Drives major interannual variability in global climate (precipitation, temperature, hurricanes). Climate-change interaction: warming trend may modify ENSO amplitude, frequency, type. CMIP6 model results split between more frequent/intense El Niños + less variability. Observations: super-El-Niños (1982, 1997, 2015, 2023) possibly more frequent recently. Walker-circulation slowdown observed since 1979 — consistent with weak-El-Niño-like background. Implications: planning under climate change must integrate both background warming + altered ENSO behavior; ENSO-sensitive regions (NE Brazil, E. Africa, Indonesia) face compounding stress. Active research + observation key.
